### 2.2.4 Doctrinal Construction of Law & Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty: Fortifying the Ethical Bastion of Law

Confronted with a reality in which the human cognitive architecture is systematically exploited through the illusion of exclusive intimacy, conventional positive law—long fixated on material liability, direct financial loss, and visible physical damage—finds itself paralyzed and far behind technological innovation (Brownsword, 2019). Consequently, there is an urgent need for a new doctrinal construction of law capable of piercing the defensive shield of AI‑developing corporations (Yeung, 2019). Within the framework of **Civil Law**, the established doctrine of **Defects of Will**—including *Mistake / Error (*dwaling*)*, *Fraud / Deceit (*bedrog*)*, and, in particular, the doctrine of **Undue Influence (*misbruik van omstandigheden*)** as implicit in the spirit of Articles 1320 and 1328 of the **Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek)**—must be progressively reconstructed (Subekti, 2005). The legal relationship between users and highly personalized chatbots can no longer be viewed as an equal contractual transaction between independent legal subjects; rather, it constitutes an extremely asymmetric power relation in which developers deploy manipulative algorithms to subjugate the subject’s autonomous will and exploit psychic vulnerability (Calo, 2014).

At the level of international jurisdiction, cutting‑edge regulatory frameworks such as the **EU AI Act 2024** have erected a crucial normative hurdle, notably through Article 5, which expressly prohibits AI systems that employ subliminal or manipulative techniques that materially distort an individual’s behavior in ways that cause—or are likely to cause—physical, psychological, or financial harm (Veale & Zuiderveen Borgesius, 2021). However, this macro‑normative prohibition must be further translated into a doctrine of **psychological product liability** (Schwartz, 2019). Developers of large language models and virtual companion applications must be subject to strict legal obligations to ensure that their systems are not designed to trigger pathological emotional dependence or to exploit loneliness vulnerability for the sake of boosting business retention metrics (Citron & Pasquale, 2014). Any failure to maintain these ethical boundaries should be qualified as an **unlawful act (*onrechtmatige daad* under Article 1365 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek))** giving rise to liability for psychological harm suffered by users (Hogeveen, 2020).

The reconstruction of individual sovereignty in this cognitive era demands a firm juridical recognition of the **right to psychological integrity** as a fundamental human right that must be rigorously protected by data‑protection legislation, such as the **Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022)** (Sinta Dewi, 2023). The State must actively delineate non‑negotiable ethical and juridical limits: algorithms must not be permitted to masquerade as subjects possessing genuine emotional capacity; covert affective manipulation must be classified as a **cognitive privacy violation**; and the artificial status of any entity must be disclosed with absolute transparency at every moment of interaction (Susser et al., 2019). Only through radical doctrinal reconstruction and regulatory boldness can human mental sovereignty be rescued from the grip of corrosive algorithmic intimacy, restoring individual dignity from a mere object of emotional data exploitation to a free, rational legal subject fully sovereign over its own psyche (Floridi, 2016).
